**The exercise hypothesis proposes that early language use preserves language-learning capacity, while the maturational-state hypothesis allows capacity to decline despite early use.** Both assume an early advantage, but they differ in what early successful experience protects.
children: Later second-language difficulty in people who already acquired a first language is more directly compatible with maturation than with complete preservation through exercise.

blocks.text: This does not make early first-language experience unimportant. Early access and age-related change address related but distinct questions.

**Mayberry, Lock and Kazmi compared later language learning after different early-language histories.** Deaf individuals without accessible early language performed worse than those who had acquired an early spoken or signed language.
children: Children first exposed to ASL at ages 9–15 had particular difficulty when it was also their first language. Those who had first learned a spoken language did much better, and the differences persisted.

blocks.text: The comparison distinguishes late first-language learning from late acquisition of an additional language.
**Semantic blocking effects must be separated from visual-recognition difficulty.** Objects from one semantic category could resemble one another visually, creating a potential confound in naming.
children: The materials were normed so that same-category items were not more visually similar on average. A separate visual-similarity manipulation also produced a different time course.

blocks.text: Visual blocking affected the first block, whereas the semantic pattern of interest developed differently. This weakens a purely visual explanation.

**Belke and colleagues presented four objects simultaneously but required their names in sequence.** This tests whether the absence of an effect in another simultaneous-display study depended on presentation format.
children: Displaying all objects at once reduces dependence on a succession of isolated pictures. Serial naming still requires selecting and producing one label after another.

blocks.text: Eye tracking provides additional timing information about the processing of each object.

**Eye movements and speech onsets provide different timing measures during serial naming.** Gaze duration records how long the eyes remain on an object, while eye–speech lag concerns the interval between leaving it and beginning its spoken name.
children: A participant can move the eyes toward the next object before articulating the current one. The measures therefore separate overlapping parts of preparation.

blocks.text: Different blocking effects on these measures can help constrain the processing stage affected.
**Semantic blocking increases gaze duration after the first presentation cycle, but not overall speech duration or eye–speech lag.** The measures therefore do not show a uniform slowdown.
children: Speech duration decreases with repetition without a blocking difference. Gaze duration shows the condition difference after the first cycle.

blocks.text: The nonsignificant lag difference should not be reported as evidence for a reversed effect. The reported pattern is interpreted as supporting a contribution at lemma selection rather than articulation or phonological encoding.

**McMurray and colleagues tested whether fine phonetic information affects lexical competition.** Participants heard a /b/–/p/ continuum while viewing pictures including BEAR and PEAR, with eye movements recorded.
children: **Voice onset time**, or VOT, varies the timing between release and voicing. It can change how strongly the sound supports /b/ or /p/.

blocks.text: A thresholded account would pass a completed categorical decision onward. A cascaded account allows graded information to influence word candidates before uncertainty is fully resolved.
**Participants selected the picture that best matched the spoken item.** Their BEAR–PEAR choices produced a typical step-like identification function across VOT.
children: Shorter VOTs favored the /b/ response and longer VOTs the /p/ response. Near the boundary, the preferred category changed rapidly.

blocks.text: A categorical-looking final response does not establish that all earlier lexical activation was categorical.
**Competitor looks vary with phonetic ambiguity even within a chosen category.** Tokens closer to the /b/–/p/ boundary produce more competition than clear tokens farther from it.
children: A participant can ultimately select BEAR while spending more time looking at PEAR when the sound is close to the boundary.

blocks.text: This supports the claim that fine phonetic information remains relevant to lexical activation, rather than disappearing completely after a categorical phoneme decision.

**Competitor fixation increases as a token approaches the category boundary from either side.** For BEAR responses, more /p/-like VOT increases looks to PEAR. For PEAR responses, more /b/-like VOT increases looks to BEAR.
children: The graph separates early and late observation windows. The gradient remains visible in the later competition measure, supporting continued sensitivity to within-category phonetic detail.

blocks.text: The result favors cascaded use of graded evidence over a model that transmits only a completed phoneme label with all within-category detail discarded.
